1422.title: the summit sit
1422.hook: a woman stands in a king's hall with his son, he says he doesn't remember her, and she doesn't leave quietly
1422.howItsDone: The women of the epics are remembered in retellings, songs, plays and household observances; Savitri, for example, is remembered by some married Hindu women in a vow kept at a banyan tree.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit went back to Ayurveda, and an old definition of health that doesn't stop at the body. Today, a new week on the summit.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `A NEW WEEK ON THE SUMMIT.`

segments.voice: A royal hall, crowded. A woman walks in from the forest with a small boy beside her. She reminds the king of his promise. He looks straight at her and says he doesn't remember her. In the Mahabharata, Shakuntala stands there, stunned and furious. Then she speaks, in his own hall, in front of everyone. That scene came near the end of a long stretch of this year with the women of the epics. Today, all of them at once.
screen: `A WOMAN IN THE KING'S HALL.` → `I DO NOT REMEMBER YOU.` → `SHE DOESN'T LEAVE QUIETLY.`

segments.voice: The epics give these women words, often at the very moment someone expects them to be silent. Told to stay home while Rama goes into exile, Sita argues: from duty, from love, and, Valmiki keeps it, with a sharp line about whether her father married her to a man at all. She wins, and goes. During the war, Gandhari's son asks her for a blessing of victory. She won't say the words he wants. She gives him a line that takes no side by name: where dharma is, there is victory. Savitri walks behind Death on the road, with no weapon and no army, only a conversation. In the epic, what pleases Yama isn't her grief or her cleverness. It's what she says about the good. Kunti, in the Bhagavata, asks Krishna for a strange gift: let the troubles come again, because in trouble she saw him. Damayanti, searching for a husband who vanished, sends no soldiers. She sends a question only he would understand. And Shakuntala, denied in that hall, tells the king that the sun, the moon and his own heart all saw what he did. Readers hear these women differently, and the tradition holds the readings side by side. Some hear devotion first: loyalty, faith, steadiness under loss. Others hear women choosing their own road, sometimes against the men trying to choose it for them. Some readers notice retellings that make them quieter than the old texts do. The texts themselves keep the lines. A row of voices, each speaking at the hour it cost the most to speak.
screen: `THE EPICS GIVE THEM WORDS.` · `SITA ARGUES, GANDHARI WON'T FLATTER.` · `SAVITRI TALKS ON THE ROAD WITH DEATH.` · `THE READINGS HELD SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `A ROW OF VOICES.`

segments.voice: Let one of these women come to mind, and let her stand there at the moment she spoke. Then notice, gently, whether there's a true thing you've been keeping quiet about; you don't have to say it, just let it be known to you, the way the sun and the moon saw. If you pray, you can bring it before God, or before the goddess, in words you already know.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the women of the epics, each given words at the hardest hour. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. What she actually said is still there in the text. See you tomorrow.

1423.title: the summit sit
1423.hook: a song closes by saying whose it is: the women who signed their own names, and the names they signed
1423.howItsDone: The songs of women saints such as Mirabai, Andal and Akka Mahadevi are still sung in homes, temples and gatherings, and some Sri Vaishnava families sing Andal's wedding song at their own weddings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit listened to the women of the epics: Sita arguing, Gandhari refusing to flatter, Savitri talking with Death.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `WHAT DID SHE ACTUALLY SAY?`

segments.voice: Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar. Mira's Lord is Giridhar, the one who lifted the mountain. That phrase closes song after song sung in Mirabai's name, like a stamp pressed into wax. Singers call it a chhap. Yesterday's women were given their words by the poets of the epics. The next stretch of the year turned to women whose own words survive, in songs and in a few lines of scripture, sometimes with their names pressed right into them.
screen: `MIRA'S LORD IS GIRIDHAR.` → `A STAMP PRESSED INTO WAX.` → `WOMEN IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Start with the names they gave their God. Mira's songs end on Giridhar. Akka Mahadevi, in Karnataka, closes her vachanas on the lord white as jasmine. Andal, in Tamil, dreams her whole wedding to the Lord, verse by verse, each one ending, I dreamed it, friend. A name for God, chosen and repeated, tells you whose voice you're hearing. Then the names they gave themselves. Karaikkal Ammaiyar's tradition says Shiva called her Mother. But in her own hymns she signs as a pey, a ghoul of the cremation ground, dancing near him in the night. She didn't hide the bones. She signed with them. Lal Ded, in Kashmir, let people curse her and others bring her flowers, and said neither could touch her. And some of these women left no songs at all, only questions, kept in an Upanishad. Gargi asks Yajnavalkya what the world is woven on, layer after layer, and when she's told to stop, she comes back later with two more questions, like a warrior stringing a bow. Maitreyi, offered a share of property, asks what she'd do with something that can't make her immortal. Without her question, the teaching that follows has no door. One honest turn. With songs that traveled mouth to mouth, nobody can always say which lines go back to the woman herself. Some readers sort older from newer. Others say a song stays alive by being sung, changing a little in every mouth. Either way, the signature keeps working. Whoever sings the song steps aside at the end: not my Lord, but Mira's Lord.
screen: `THE NAMES THEY GAVE THEIR GOD.` · `THE NAMES THEY GAVE THEMSELVES.` · `GARGI AND MAITREYI: THE QUESTIONS.` · `THE SINGER STEPS ASIDE.` · then, large: `NOT MY LORD, BUT MIRA'S LORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one of these voices, Mira, Akka, Andal, Lal Ded, Gargi, Maitreyi or Karaikkal Ammaiyar, and let her signature stand in the quiet for a moment. Then, at the end of each out-breath, notice whose name rises in you, a person's, a place's or no name at all, and let it go. If you pray, you can rest in the name of God you already use.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the women in their own words, and the names they signed. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. A name at the end of a song tells you whose it is. Rest well.

1424.title: the summit sit
1424.hook: palm leaves in a locked room, a clay goddess going back to the river, sandals in a palanquin: what each region carries
1424.howItsDone: Regional festivals and pilgrimages such as Durga Puja in Bengal, the Pandharpur wari in Maharashtra, Herath in Kashmir and the Sabarimala pilgrimage in Kerala are kept by families and communities in their own languages and customs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit went back to the women in their own words, and the names they signed.

Palm leaves in a locked temple room, half eaten by ants. A goddess shaped from river clay, welcomed home like a daughter and then carried back to the water. A silver palanquin in a sea of white caps, and inside it, a pair of sandals. A cloth bundle on a pilgrim's head. Walnuts soaked through the night and handed to the neighbors. The year held each, one region at a time. Today, the last of the summit sits: what each place carries.
screen: `PALM LEAVES AND RIVER CLAY.` → `SANDALS IN A PALANQUIN.` → `WHAT EACH PLACE CARRIES.`

segments.voice: In Tamil country, the story of the Tevaram: palm leaves found in a locked room, much of them eaten away, and a voice saying what this age needs has been kept. In Bengal, Durga in clay, who is also Uma, a daughter come home to her worried mother, and sent back to the river when the festival ends. In Maharashtra, the Varkaris walk to Pandharpur with the sandals of their saints, because the sandals stand for the one who walked in them. In Kashmir, pots of water and walnuts kept through Shiva's great night, and the walnuts shared out the next day. In Kerala, the bundle on the pilgrim's head on the climb to Sabarimala: offerings in one part, food for the road in the other. In Gujarat, a letter of daily conduct, written by a teacher for people he would never meet. In Punjab, a song by Namdev, a tailor from Maharashtra, kept in the Sikh scripture, about a boy whose mind stays on his kite string. Each belongs to its own place, language and community, and this year let each one speak in its own words. They aren't lined up from lesser to greater, or melted into one. Still, look at what the objects do. Almost every one is carried, handed on or shared: leaves kept, a daughter sent off, sandals borne along a road, a bundle on a head, walnuts given next door, a letter sent ahead, a song that traveled north. A tradition that lives in many places lives, in part, by things passed from hand to hand.

Stay with that short chain for a few breaths, then think of someone you might hand something to, one day. If you pray, you can offer that thing, and that person, to God in your own way.

1425.title: Year 4: year close
1425.hook: the summit sit, looking back over a year that kept asking questions, from a king in a forest to a hymn that wonders who really knows
1425.howItsDone: Hindu traditions keep questions inside their texts: the Upanishads hold dialogues between teachers and questioners, and the hymn of creation, with its open last line, is chanted as part of the Rig Veda.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last summit sit: the regional traditions, and what each place carries, from palm leaves to walnuts. Today, the whole year at once.

Who really knows? The hymn of creation in the Rig Veda asks it near its end, and then, in paraphrase, says this about the one who watches over everything from the highest heaven: perhaps he knows, or perhaps he does not know. That hymn stands in the scripture, question and all. And from the top of year four, it doesn't sit alone. This whole year kept stopping at questions. Today, the year close, told by the questions it asked.
screen: `WHO REALLY KNOWS?` → `PERHAPS HE DOES NOT KNOW.` → `A YEAR OF QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: It opened with one. A king who'd lost his kingdom and a merchant thrown out by his family asked a sage: we know these things have left us, so why doesn't knowing help? The whole Devi Mahatmya is the answer. Then the questions got sharper. The schools of thought asked how anyone knows anything at all, and the path let each school answer in its own way, ranking none. The Nyaya Sutra, near its opening, names the means of knowing. The Vedas asked in their own voice: what covered it, where, in whose keeping? Then came the women, and several of them were remembered for a question. Gargi asked Yajnavalkya what the world is woven on, and when he told her to stop, she came back with two more. Maitreyi asked what she'd do with wealth that can't make her immortal. Damayanti found her husband by sending out a question only he would understand. Even the regions brought one: a Kashmiri teacher, Abhinavagupta, asking why a sad play leaves its audience lighter. A tradition could have smoothed these over and kept only the answers. This one kept the questions inside its sacred texts: in the king's mouth, in Gargi's, in a Vedic hymn. And some are never closed. The hymn of creation doesn't resolve its last line. It ends on perhaps. So that's year four from the top: the goddess, Shiva, the schools, the three paths, the Vedas, Ayurveda as a lens, the women, the regions. And running through them, people asking honest questions out loud, and the tradition keeping them.
screen: `IT OPENED WITH ONE QUESTION.` · `THE SCHOOLS ASKED HOW WE KNOW.` · `GARGI, MAITREYI, DAMAYANTI ASKED.` · `THE QUESTIONS WERE KEPT.` · then, large: `IT ENDS ON PERHAPS.`

segments.voice: Let one real question rise, something you don't know the answer to, about your life, or about God, or about anything, and let it sit beside you the way the hymn lets its last line sit. Each time the mind starts building an answer, come back to the breath, and to the question, still open. If you pray, you can hold it before God, or the goddess, as it is.
Year four. The goddess, Shiva, the schools of thought, the Vedas, the women and the regions, looked at from the top by the questions they asked. Today's word.
Your line: Year 4, year close. Tomorrow, the last day of the year, and the ranges ahead. I'll be here tomorrow.

1426.title: year 4 · the ranges
1426.hook: this part of the path is still being planned: a scribe who won't let the pen stop, and a poet who asks him to understand every line first
1426.howItsDone: In Hindu tradition, Ganesha is remembered at the start of a new undertaking, a journey, a book, a school year or a ceremony, and some images show him as a scribe with a broken tusk.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Year 4, year close: a year that kept asking questions, and a hymn that ends on perhaps. Today is the last day of year four.

A poet has a story too long to write down himself, so he asks for a scribe. The one who comes is Ganesha. Tradition tells it this way: Vyasa has the Mahabharata in his mind, and Ganesha agrees to write it on one condition. Once the pen starts, it must not stop. Vyasa agrees, and adds a condition of his own: Ganesha must understand every line before he writes it. A good story for the last day of year four, standing on a ridge with more ranges in view, and the next one starting with letters.
screen: `A POET WHO NEEDS A SCRIBE.` → `THE PEN MUST NOT STOP.` → `UNDERSTAND EVERY LINE FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the view, said plainly. The next ranges are drawn on the map. Year five begins with Sanskrit for readers: the script, a few words, enough to look at a verse and recognize it. Then come the Puranas, the dharma texts read critically, the Tantras with careful framing, a service capstone, Hinduism around the world, and the great sayings of the Upanishads. That's the outline. The lessons themselves are still being written and checked. Now back to the scribe. The story is a bargain between two kinds of care. Ganesha's condition is about keeping going: no stopping, no waiting around. Vyasa's is about slowing down: nothing written that isn't understood. And tradition adds that whenever Vyasa needed time to think, he'd say a verse so knotted that even Ganesha had to pause to work it out. So the bargain holds both, momentum and understanding, and neither one wins. One more turn. Ganesha, the one honored at beginnings, the remover of obstacles, appears here not clearing a road but bent over a page, listening. In some tellings, when his pen breaks mid-story, he snaps off his own tusk and keeps writing, which is why he's pictured with one broken. Whatever a reader makes of that, it's a picture of how a long work actually gets done: a little at a time, without quitting, and without pretending to understand what you don't. Tomorrow, year five starts small, with the letters themselves. A good place for a scribe to begin.

segments.voice: With one fingertip, trace a slow line on your palm or on the table, as if writing a single letter, one stroke to a breath, noticing each stroke as it's made. If the mind runs ahead to next year, bring it back to this one line. If you pray, you can begin by remembering Ganesha, honored in Hindu tradition at beginnings.
Year four. The goddess, Shiva, the schools, the Vedas, the women and the regions, now walked. And the ranges beyond, drawn on the map, still being written. Today's word.
Your line: year four, the ranges. Tomorrow, the letters, and the first steps of a new range. Year four, done.

fork.setup: you're Ganesha. Vyasa asks you to write down the whole Mahabharata as he speaks it. what's your condition?
options: you'll write only in the mornings.
once the pen starts, it must not stop.
you'll write only the parts you like.
fork.reveal: tradition says Ganesha's condition was that the pen never stop, and Vyasa added his own: understand every line before writing it.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: gaṇeśa, lord of the ganas, honored at beginnings, and here the scribe.

what it means: in the Mahabharata's scribe story he is also the one who writes, under a bargain of momentum and understanding.
what a scholar hears: the scribe story is held as tradition, a picture of the epic as something both spoken without stopping and understood line by line.

chat.says: What deal did Ganesha and Vyasa make about writing down the Mahabharata?
options: Ganesha's pen must not stop, and Vyasa said he must understand every line first.
Ganesha would write only in the mornings, and Vyasa could stop when he liked.
Ganesha would write fast and skip lines, and Vyasa would fill the gaps later.
chat.meaning: In the scribe story, Ganesha's pen must not stop, and Vyasa's condition is that he understand every line: momentum and understanding.
